title: Cap. X Arg. IV: whoever has power over the necessary antecedent has power over the consequent — if believing/not believing from free will excited by sufficient grace is the antecedent to election/reprobation, each can choose either
pass_a_gloss: That is thence evinced, because in whose power the necessary antecedent is, in the same one's also is the consequent, which depends infallibly from the same antecedent: If therefore to believe, and to embrace offered grace, be the necessary antecedent unto election, and not to believe, or finally to refuse offered grace, be the antecedent unto reprobation, and both of these depend from a free act of the human will excited by sufficient grace, what is more open than that it is in the power of singular persons that they be reprobated or not reprobated, since between these as contradictories a middle can by no means be assigned?
pass_b_english: That is proved thus: whoever has power over the necessary antecedent also has power over the consequent that depends infallibly on it. So if believing and embracing offered grace is the necessary antecedent to election, and not believing — or finally refusing offered grace — is the antecedent to reprobation, and both hang on a free act of the human will excited by sufficient grace, what is plainer than that it lies in each one's power to be reprobated or not? Between those as contradictories no middle can be assigned.
source_text: Id inde evincitur, quia in cujus potestate est antecedens necessarium, in ejusdem etiam est consequens, quod ex eodem antecedente infallibiliter dependet: Si igitur credere, et gratiam oblatam amplecti sit antecedens necessarium ad electionem, et non credere, seu gratiam oblatam finaliter respuere sit antecedens ad reprobationem, et utrumque horum ex libero actu humanae voluntatis sufficienti gratia excitatae dependeat, quid apertius quam esse in potestate singulorum ut reprobentur vel non reprobentur, cum inter haec tanquam contradictoria medium assignari nullo modo possit?
